Monitoring key physiological metrics, including heart rate and heart rate variability, has been shown to be of value in exercise science, disease management, and overall health. The purpose of this study was to investigate the diurnal variation of physiological responses and physical performances using digital biomarkers as a precise measurement tool during a walking football match (WFM) in higher-weight men. Nineteen males (mean age: 42.53 ± 12.18 years; BMI: 33.31 ± 4.31 kg·m −2 ) were engaged in a WFM at two different times of the day. Comprehensive evaluations of physiological parameters (e.g., cardiac autonomic function, lactate, glycemia, and oxygen saturation), along with physical performance, were assessed before, during, and after the match. Overall, there was a significant interaction (time of day x WFM) for mean blood pressure (MBP) ( p = 0.007) and glycemia ( p = 0.039). Glycemia decreased exclusively in the evening after WFM ( p = 0.001), while mean blood pressure did not significantly change. Rating of perceived exertion was significantly higher in the evening than in the morning ( p = 0.04), while the heart rate recovery after 1 min (HRR60s) of the match was lower in the evening than in the morning ( p = 0.048). Overall, walking football practice seems to be safe, whatever the time of day. Furthermore, HRR60, glycemia, and (MBP) values were lower in the evening compared to the morning, suggesting that evening exercise practice could be safer for individuals with higher weight. The utilization of digital biomarkers for monitoring health status during WFM has been shown to be efficient. recreational soccer circadian rhythms HRV metabolic health This research received no external funding. 1. Introduction Obesity, often associated with sedentary behavior [ 1 , 2 ], is linked to a high risk of cardiovascular, metabolic, and pulmonary diseases [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 ]. This chronic disorder is currently ranked as the 5th highest global public health problem and is responsible for 4.8% of deaths worldwide [ 7 ]. Mainly, Tunisian statistics indicate a prevalence of 26.2% for obesity [ 8 ]. Particularly, obesity is associated with circadian misalignment, which can be explained by social jet lag and an erratic lifestyle [ 9 ]. Indeed, the circadian clock system is involved in controlling the biology of adipose tissue, energy metabolism, and physiological responses to exercise [ 10 ]. Due to its chronobiotic effects, exercise can induce a phase shift in the circadian rhythmicity of the supra-chiasmatic nucleus [ 11 , 12 ], which could lessen the harmful effects of circadian misalignment [ 13 , 14 ], and increase the activation of metabolic pathways and systemic energy homeostasis in skeletal muscle [ 15 ]. Moreover, exercise is effective in improving hunger suppression as a result of changes in energy balance [ 16 ]. For these reasons, regular physical activity is strongly encouraged in order to minimize the consequences of obesity and to fight against other cardiovascular and metabolic disorders [ 17 ]. In this context, recreational team sports, particularly football, have emerged as cost-effective interventions promoting cardiometabolic health [ 18 , 19 , 20 , 21 ]. Walking football (WF), a variant introduced in 2011, is a feasible and sustainable exercise intervention. WF involves intermittent activity with frequent direction changes and walking pace, following an acyclic pattern. Furthermore, players must always walk and not run during a WF match (WFM). Research has demonstrated that during a 1 h WFM, participants covered a distance of 2.5 miles [ 22 ], maintained a walking cadence averaging 44–63 steps per minute [ 23 ], and made an average of 100 changes of direction [ 24 ]. Research suggests the potential of WF practice to enhance participants’ body composition and physical fitness [ 25 , 26 ], while also contributing positively to mental well-being [ 27 , 28 , 29 ]. Mainly, it has been demonstrated that timed exercises can have a greater physiological and molecular responses, promoting chronobiological homeostasis and treating conditions like obesity [ 12 , 30 ]. Understanding the time-of-day (TOD)-dependent physiological responses to WFM is crucial for robust evidence-backed guidelines and clinical recommendations. Regarding cardiovascular responses, previous studies have shown that exercise in the afternoon or in the evening presents a greater glucose reduction than in the morning [ 31 , 32 ]. Moreover, it has been demonstrated that performing 60 min of endurance exercise in the evening resulted in a significant elevation of blood adrenaline levels immediately post-exercise, as compared to the morning [ 33 ]. Additionally, previous studies have indicated that cardiovascular responses to exercise are TOD-dependent [ 34 ]. Despite substantial evidence of the positive impact of physical activity on reducing mortality risk [ 34 , 35 , 36 ], knowledge is limited regarding the potential cardiometabolic benefits of WF practice at different TODs. Recognizing this gap, our focus in this study was on assessing physiological responses and physical performance during a single WFM conducted at different TODs in men with higher body weight. This exploration aims to provide valuable insights into the recommendations on the how and when of exercise, especially in the context of higher-weight individuals.

extracted_data.document_summary: This study investigated the time-of-day-dependent physiological, physical, and psychological responses of higher-weight men to a Walking Football Match (WFM). Findings revealed that evening WFM led to significantly lower glycemia, mean blood pressure (MBP), and heart rate recovery after 1 minute (HRR60s) compared to morning sessions, suggesting potential safety and metabolic benefits for higher-weight individuals when exercising in the evening. Most other parameters, including HRV, lactate, SpO2, and various physical performance metrics, showed no significant diurnal variation.

treatment_details.dose_specificity: Participants engaged in a single session of 5 vs. 5 Walking Football Matches (WFM) on artificial turf fields. Each session lasted approximately one hour, comprising a 10-min warm-up, two 20-min playing periods separated by a 10-min passive recovery, and a 5-min cool-down. Matches were performed in randomized order, either in the morning (6:30 a.m. - 8:30 a.m.) or in the evening (5:00 p.m. - 7:00 p.m.), with 7 days between sessions. The activity was classified as moderate intensity (4.85-4.9 METs), with participants averaging around 2500-2600 steps per session and a cadence of approximately 63.8 steps/min. The study primarily focused on time-of-day effects, with no explicit dose-response comparisons regarding WFM intensity or duration.

measured_effect.direction_of_change: Lower (less pronounced increase) in the evening WFM session compared to the morning WFM session
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Significant interaction (time of day x WFM) (p = 0.007); MBP values were lower in the evening compared to the morning; WFM-induced increase in MBP was more pronounced in the morning compared to the evening.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Regulation of systemic blood circulation and cardiovascular function, influenced by the sympathetic nervous system.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: During and after Walking Football Match (WFM) performed at different times of day (morning vs. evening) in higher-weight men.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates cardiovascular health status and suggests that practicing WFM in the evening is safer due to a less pronounced MBP increase, offering potential safety benefits for higher-weight individuals.

analyzed_biomarkers.measured_tissue_or_fluid: Blood (from the tip of the index finger)

measured_effect.direction_of_change: Lower; decreased exclusively in the evening after WFM, with a greater reduction compared to the morning session.
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Significant interaction (time of day x WFM) (p = 0.039; ES = 0.21); decreased exclusively in the evening after WFM (p = 0.001); overall values were lower in the evening compared to the morning.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Regulation of blood sugar levels and energy metabolism, influenced by hormones like catecholamines and IL-6.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Post-Walking Football Match (WFM) performed at different times of day (morning vs. evening) in higher-weight men.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates the body's metabolic response to exercise and glucose utilization, suggesting evening exercise could be safer for higher-weight individuals due to improved glucose regulation and greater blood glucose control/insulin sensitivity, particularly relevant for metabolic health.

measured_effect.direction_of_change: Higher in the evening compared to the morning
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Significantly higher in the evening than in the morning (p = 0.04; d = 0.47). Values obtained during WFM indicated moderate (≥4) to very hard intensity (≥7).

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Subjective assessment of exercise intensity, effort, and physiological stress.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: During Walking Football Match (WFM) performed at different times of day (morning vs. evening) in higher-weight men.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates that the same walking football activity is perceived as more strenuous when performed in the evening, and can guide appropriate exercise levels for cardiorespiratory and musculoskeletal capacity.

measured_effect.direction_of_change: Lower in the evening compared to the morning
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Lower in the evening than in the morning (p = 0.048; d = 0.47); overall values were lower in the evening compared to the morning. Previous study reported 27 ± 7 bpm in morning, 29 ± 7 bpm in evening among hypertensive men.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Reflects cardiac autonomic function, post-exercise cardiac autonomic recovery, and sympathetic activity, indicating cardiovascular fitness/recovery capacity.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Post-Walking Football Match (WFM) recovery, comparing evening vs. morning sessions in higher-weight men.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates safety of exercise and is correlated with mortality risk (low HRR values). Lower HRR60s values in the evening compared to the morning suggest that evening exercise practice could be safer for individuals with higher weight.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Increased after the WFM at both morning and evening sessions. A previous study revealed a significant increase of around 157% post-session. No significant diurnal variation noted.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Indicator of glycolytic pathway activity and energy metabolism during exercise.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: After Walking Football Match, in both morning and evening sessions in higher-weight men.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Highlights the high intensity of WFM, indicating significant demand on the glycolytic pathway.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Lack of significant interaction between TOD and WFM for time domain parameters (mean RR, SDNN, and RMSSD) and frequency domain parameters. HRV biomarkers were influenced by the WFM, exhibiting a time-dependent recovery to pre-exercise levels. TOD did not affect HR and HRV recovery after WFM.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Assesses cardiac autonomic function and the balance between sympathetic and parasympathetic nervous systems.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Before and after Walking Football Match, comparing morning vs. evening sessions in higher-weight men.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Useful tool in assessing the risk of cardiac events and in evaluating the advantages/disadvantages linked to physical exercise. Decreased HRV indicates altered cardiac autonomic function in obesity.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: No significant difference between the two TODs for mean HR (p = 0.40, d = 0.19) and HR max (p = 0.60, d = 0.03). Mean HR during WFM: 133.54 beat/min in the morning and 136.54 in the evening.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Indicator of cardiac activity and exercise intensity.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: During Walking Football Match, comparing morning vs. evening sessions in higher-weight men.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates level of physical activity and cardiovascular exertion during exercise.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: No significant difference between the two TODs (p = 0.54, d = 0.17). Participants achieved an average of 2546.94 ± 412.37 steps in the morning and 2611.38 ± 356.34 steps in the evening.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Measures the volume of walking activity.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: During Walking Football Match, comparing morning vs. evening sessions in higher-weight men.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Helps in meeting daily step count recommendations and achieving moderate-to-vigorous intensity activity.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: No significant difference between the two TODs (p = 0.18, d = 0.08). Values were 4.85 ± 0.62 in the morning and 4.9 ± 0.46 in the evening, corresponding to moderate exercise intensity (3–6 METs).

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Reflects energy expenditure during physical activity relative to resting metabolic rate.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: During Walking Football Match, comparing morning vs. evening sessions in higher-weight men.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Classifies the intensity of physical activity (moderate) for health and fitness recommendations.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: No significant interaction (TOD × Match) for FAS. Participant’s psychological condition did not vary significantly between morning and evening sessions.
